title: How the Latest AI Leap Is Disrupting Business Models
dek: A developer one-shots Photoshop with a Claude subscription, AI-accelerated crackers jailbreak the PS5, and mashed-up AAA games are suddenly a one-day project. The Astra and Opus 5.5 jump has turned decompiling and reconstituting software from a legal curiosity into a mass capability — and today's episode is about how Adobe, Epic, Xbox, Bumble's new owners, and even David's Bridal are responding to business models being torn up in real time.

oneIdea.headline: When models can decompile anything, business models have to evolve or die.
oneIdea.summary: Late 2025's model jump looked incremental until it birthed the agent era. Astra and Opus 5.5 feel like the same kind of moment: clean-room rebuilds of Photoshop, jailbroken consoles, and playable game mashups delivered in a day. The lesson emerging from Epic's handwritten-code ban, Xbox's new lab, and the PE firms rebuilding Bumble and Bending Spoons' brands around AI isn't that software is over — it's that legacy players now believe change is the name of the game, and they have to evolve to survive.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Software you can rebuild is software you must govern
items.body: The developer who rebuilt Photoshop with an AI model, and Chamath's claim that software IP is worthless, are mostly about commercial products. Whittemore thinks this is overstated, because most customers pay for support and maintenance. For practices the practical point is that clinical systems are bought for assurance, updates and accountability, not code. A home-built tool still needs DCB0129 or DCB0160 safety cases, a data protection assessment and an owner. Zitron would add that cheap building has not made cheap running.

items.title: Banks hiring people to patch what AI finds
items.body: Bank of America hired a thousand contractors to patch vulnerabilities found by an AI security model, and Jamie Dimon says cyber risk has risen tenfold. NHS practices run ageing systems and shared accounts, and the same tools can be used to scan them. Keep software patched, use multi-factor sign-in, check backups, and ask suppliers how they respond to newly found vulnerabilities.

items.title: Anthropic's figures and procurement
items.body: Both positions agree that the headline numbers are unaudited and uncertain. A scribe or triage tool built on a lab that may be loss-making or may be extremely profitable carries supplier risk. In contracts, look for data export, exit terms and price caps, so a practice can switch if prices or ownership change. Little else here bears directly on the NHS.

the_other_side.text: Zitron's piece from two days before argues that 'annualized' revenue is marketing rather than accounting, and compares it with reported quarters: he puts Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue at about 15.5 billion dollars, far below its headline run rates. He says labs' growth leans on venture-funded startups buying tokens at a loss, and that GPU contract prices may not cover depreciation. He does not write about decompiling software or Photoshop, so this addresses the edition's earnings and compute items rather than its lead.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether AI revenue is real, durable and profitable, or partly a product of subsidy and accounting choices. Both accept as fact that Anthropic told investors of 16.8 billion dollars in unaudited Q3 revenue, that CoreWeave's bonds trade near distressed levels, and that compute commitments run to hundreds of billions. The empirical question is whether audited figures confirm that growth, margins and cash flow; the observable is Anthropic's IPO filing and whether Q4 reaches the roughly 57 per cent growth needed for 110 billion dollars annualised. The residue is worldview: whether disruption of old business models justifies the spending. For Whittemore to be vindicated, Q4 and audited numbers must hold up and legacy firms must adapt profitably. For Zitron, filings must show weak margins or revenue propped by subsidised resale. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron certain of a bubble and anti-hype. The signal is that both distrust unaudited figures. Watch what Anthropic's IPO filing actually discloses.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's $16.8B quarter gets the full earnings-day treatment
headlines.summary: At a pre-IPO investor day, Anthropic told institutional money managers they did $16.8 billion in actual Q3 revenue, up 45% from Q2 — with 85% adjusted gross margins, 11% adjusted operating margins, and positive free cash flow. The market treated unaudited numbers from a private company like the most important earnings report in the world: some analysts called it a flop as tech sold off, while others marveled that 50% quarter-over-quarter growth could read as underperformance.

headlines.headline: The $110B target is a bet on Fable 5.5
headlines.summary: Reuters reports Anthropic expects $110 billion in annualized revenue by year-end — but Q3 extrapolates to just $70 billion, implying another 57% growth spurt in Q4. With live revenue trackers showing flat growth since late July, the math only works if the next model release, reportedly Fable 5.5, is a hit.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's IPO window has an accounting quirk
headlines.summary: The company can go public at its targeted $2 trillion valuation with financial disclosures up to 134 days old — meaning it may only need to include Q1 and Q2, leaving Wednesday's unaudited Q3 figures as the freshest information the market gets. Right now is the window to get the deal done at top dollar.

headlines.headline: CoreWeave bonds hit distressed levels as insiders keep selling
headlines.summary: Unsecured 2032 bonds plunged to 80 cents on the dollar — a 15% implied rate pricing serious default risk — while the stock fell another 15%. Analyst Gil Luria, who calls CoreWeave the 'subprime tranche' of AI, warns borrowing at 9% to earn 5% on increasingly commoditized data centers destroys value at every turn. CEO Mike Intrator says the market misunderstands the business, but SEC filings show he's sold stock every week since April.

headlines.headline: ASML can't meet AI chip-tool demand for years
headlines.summary: The EUV lithography monopolist says demand is running way ahead of its planned 30% capacity boost, with TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix, and Musk's Terafab all expanding at once. Some customer reservations stretch into 2029 and even 2039, and the CFO says it would be 'extremely hard' to add tremendous capacity by 2028 'even if we started digging today.'

headlines.headline: Advancing capability and advancing safety are not in conflict. They are, in fact, one.
headlines.attribution: Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO, during UK press appearances
headlines.summary: Pressed across a day of UK appearances, the Nvidia CEO said he would hypothetically cut off chips to an irresponsible AI developer — after a conversation — while pushing back on a journalist's framing that he thinks safety is solved: 'Between now and the end of humanity, we're going to have a lot of work to do.'

headlines.headline: Call Jensen an AI realist
headlines.summary: NLW's coinage for Huang's position: safety risks are real but tractable, an engineering problem to be engaged with engineering rather than politics — not a world of neatly opposed pro-safety and anti-safety camps. Demonstrating the point, NVIDIA announced $250 million in compute over five years for UK safety research.

headlines.headline: AI is causing a banking hiring boom — to patch the bugs it exposes
headlines.summary: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to support 3,000 staff patching vulnerabilities revealed by Mythos, driving hundreds of millions in extra Q3 costs. It echoes Jamie Dimon's comment that cyber risk in banking went up 'tenfold' after Mythos — JPMorgan isn't getting hysterical, it's 'rolling up our sleeves and going to work to fix it.'

headlines.headline: The OpenAI bugging suspect was one day from fleeing
headlines.summary: The employee accused of planting a listening device had booked a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for October 12; the DOJ's sealed indictment enabled an arrest the day after the warrant issued. The labs have been vigilant for years — OpenAI's onboarding includes an entire section on detecting insider threats and recognizing intelligence agents, who have posed as everything from bar patrons to playground families.

headlines.headline: Russia fines its first AI bear
headlines.summary: A viral AI-generated image of a bear roaming a remote village triggered a real animal-control hunt. Once the village was confirmed bear-free, the woman who confessed to the prank was fined 15,000 rubles — about $178.

headlines.headline: 'Software is over': a developer one-shots Photoshop
headlines.summary: Brandon Thomas used Claude Opus to decompile Photoshop and reconstruct it as a clean-room rebuild — a copyright workaround that used to require two teams of engineers and is now practical for an individual. He's since bootlegged the entire Adobe suite and offers a buggy but free version of software Adobe prices at $100 a month; Adobe stock opened 3% lower when the story went viral.

headlines.headline: Chamath declares software IP 'effectively rendered worthless'
headlines.summary: On All-In, Palihapitiya argued that once everything is headless, wrapped in agent tools, and connected via MCP, 'the value of IP does no longer exist in software' — and says his own AI SaaS business has stopped negotiating to retain IP when building for clients, calling it 'a who cares thing.'

headlines.headline: Maybe a little podcast hyperbolic: SaaS sells support, not software
headlines.summary: People have pirated Adobe for decades without denting the business. Most SaaS companies sell the ability for IT procurement to offload maintenance for a reasonable monthly fee — and this feels like a rerun of the vibe-coding narrative, nine months after which most companies that experimented with prompting their own CRM quietly returned to their Salesforce contracts.

headlines.headline: Decompiling hit gaming like a freight train
headlines.summary: Enterprise SaaS may be fine, but AAA gaming — already in a severe downturn with console sales at a 13-year low and tens of thousands laid off — faces a different threat. What started as lighthearted mashups like Super Mario x Elden Ring escalated to AI-accelerated crackers jailbreaking the PS5 to play games from basically any system.

headlines.headline: Bloomberg Intelligence: consoles are becoming record players
headlines.summary: The thesis: AI-enabled AAA games are better served from data centers than a GPU in a plastic box, while semiconductor competition pushes hardware prices up — the base PS5 is now $650 versus $500 at launch, and the Steam Machine costs $1,000. Consoles shift from gaming's main gateway to one relatively uneconomic access point for enthusiasts and collectors.

headlines.headline: The one-person AAA studio is one to two years away — or less
headlines.summary: Game engine developer George Kal says Opus 5.5 is 'scary good' at game dev across code, shaders, system design, sounds, and debugging, predicting every solo dev ships the game in their head within one to two years with only taste and audience as moats. Elon Musk quibbled with the timeline: 'Next year.'

headlines.headline: The end game isn't competing with studios — it's not needing them
headlines.summary: The sharpest framing circulating: mashups so good people won't post them for fear of lawsuits, and an endgame where your model codes the AAA game you want, in your genre, with your aesthetics — the Genie vision of games tailored to you for the price of a subscription. If that happens at scale, the virulently anti-AI game industry gets blindsided: not competition, destruction.

headlines.headline: Epic bans handwritten code
headlines.summary: Epic Games went beyond AI-as-productivity-enhancer this week with a mandate against handwritten code, and delayed its Marvel-and-Star-Wars Disney shooter to switch to an AI-first production model — down to art generated with full AI workflows. Sweeney says the aim isn't fewer people doing the same stuff, but everyone building more and better.

headlines.headline: Much of the room wants it to be 2016 again, but it's not.
headlines.attribution: Tim Sweeney, Epic Games CEO, replying to indie dev Andre Apancsek
headlines.summary: When an indie dev told the Epic CEO his 'inability to read the room is really, really astounding,' Sweeney fired back: as the provider of tools to much of the industry, Epic has to 'design for the present that is and the future that will soon be' — and he sees it as empowering for creators.

headlines.headline: Epic's proudly vibe-coded launcher ships fast — and glitchy
headlines.summary: Epic released a new games launcher it described as vibe coded, boasting significantly faster launch times than Steam: 'Will it have some bugs? Yes. Do we wanna hear about them? Hell yes.' Gamers obliged with a flood of visual glitches — but the speedup was real.

headlines.headline: Xbox starts a lab instead of calling the lawyers
headlines.summary: CEO Asha Sharma's memo names the wave of decompiled games directly, calling accessibility, revived old games, and players-as-creators 'unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when and sometimes because they challenge our existing business models' — and launches Xbox Labs, a skunkworks building in the open. MIT's Christian Catalini called it a masterclass in what to do when AI tears up the rules your business was built on.

headlines.headline: Bumble goes private on an AI-rebuild thesis
headlines.summary: Ithaca Holdings — ex-Sequoia partner Ravi Gupta and ex-Meta CRO John Hegeman — closed a billion-dollar take-private of the struggling dating app, down 95% from its $14 billion peak. The thesis: as intelligence becomes abundant, meaningful connection becomes more precious. Investor Sarah Guo argues a tiny, fast, 'extremely AI-pilled' team with full ownership can rebuild whole companies around the technology.

headlines.headline: Berkshire doubles down on the AI-refurbish playbook
headlines.summary: Warren Buffett's firm put $330 million into Bending Spoons via private placement — on top of $600 million at the July IPO, taking its stake to 4% — and the stock soared 40%. Bending Spoons' thesis: brands like AOL, Vimeo, Evernote, and Airtable still have revenue and viable products; aggregate staff and use AI to cut maintenance costs, and legacy performance improves.

headlines.headline: David's Bridal built a wedding-planning agent with tens, not hundreds
headlines.summary: After 76 years of only selling dresses and a 2023 bankruptcy, the country's largest wedding dress retailer is pivoting 180 degrees into AI-powered wedding planning — a marketplace play with an agentic twist, anchored on first-party bride data. President Elena Vilk says what would have taken 100-plus people was built with tens using standard agentic coding tools: 'There's no way we could have achieved anything like this even three years ago.'

headlines.headline: The pattern repeats: another model jump, another unlock
headlines.summary: Opus 4.5 at the end of last year brought agents to the fore; Astra and Opus 5.5 are unlocking the decompilation era. Be cautious about prognostications of rapid change — but the legacy players themselves clearly believe change is now the name of the game, with inevitable pain and a lot of interesting new opportunities along the way.
